While on the way to the airport, Yeltsin decided to take an unannounced visit to a grocery store.[12][41] Yeltsin said that he wanted to visit a typical store in order to see what the average American shopping experience was like.[32] The group decided to visit Randalls #30 at 570 El Dorado Boulevard, near the intersection with State Highway 3,[51][47][48][49] in Webster.[32] The store manager received a phone call from the group shortly before their arrival, and he was given about 15 minutes to prepare.[32][48] The visit was a low-key event, without heavy security or media presence,[48] with the exception of reporter Stefanie Asin of the Houston Chronicle.[49][48][46] Yeltsin arrived at the store around 1:30 p.m.[41] During his visit, Yeltsin inspected the product selection in the store and tried free samples of cheese and produce.[50][52] According to the manager on duty at the time, Yeltsin was very interested in the frozen food section,[48] and a picture of Yeltsin looking at a selection of Pudding Pops was widely republished.[49][52][32] He was astonished by the selection available in the store, which he was told offered about 30,000 unique products, and expressed disbelief that such a store was available to residents outside of major urban areas like New York City.[53][49] He also asked the store manager if he had required specialized training to earn his position.[46] Speaking through an interpreter, Yeltsin talked to employees and customers,[48] asking them questions about how much they spent on groceries compared to what their salary was.[46] In total, the trip lasted about 20 minutes,[50][52][54][55] with Yeltsin receiving a goodie bag from the store staff before leaving.[49]

Following the grocery store visit, Yeltsin and his entourage flew to Miami, their final location before returning to the Soviet Union.[56][46][49] During the flight, Yeltsin was in a state of shock regarding the grocery store and remained speechless for a long time.[56] According to Sukhanov, it was during the flight that "the last vestige of Bolshevism collapsed inside" Yeltsin.[56] Following his silence, Yeltsin asked aloud, "What have they done to our people?", questioning the Soviet Union's struggles with food.[56] In a later biography, Yeltsin commented regarding his grocery store visit,[46][32]

text:
Cute creatures rotten politics hedgehogs replace royals

It tells you everything about Britain in 2026 that the Bank of England has chosen a hedgehog to grace its new polymer notes. Not a Prime Minister, not a statesman, not the new King, not BREXIT, not even a cultural giant — but a small, endangered mammal. The symbolism is not accidental. It is symptomatic of a political class so discredited, a monarchy so contested, and a national story so fractured that the safest option is to retreat into wildlife nostalgia.  

The Hedgehog as Political Escape
The hedgehog is harmless, uncontroversial, and conveniently mute. It cannot embarrass the government with scandal, nor remind the public of Brexit’s economic wreckage. It is the perfect mascot for a political establishment desperate to avoid confrontation with its own failures. By putting hedgehogs on banknotes, Britain signals that it has no human figures left who can unify the nation without provoking ridicule.  

Prime Ministers Too Toxic
Consider the recent roll call of leaders: Johnson, remembered for lies and lockdown parties; Truss, for tanking the economy in 44 days; Sunak, for presiding over stagnation. None of these figures could plausibly appear on currency without becoming a punchline. Banknotes are supposed to project stability. Britain’s leaders project chaos.  

No Gaza Genocide
Keir Starmer is the embodiment of Britain’s political emptiness. Marketed as a “safe pair of hands,” he has hollowed Labour into a party of managerial platitudes. His refusal to back striking workers, his silence on Gaza until outrage forced a shift, and his fixation on fiscal “credibility” expose a leader more concerned with appeasing elites than representing ordinary people. Definitely not suitable on the new bank notes.

Brexit as National Embarrassment
Brexit was sold as sovereignty but delivered supply chain crises, trade barriers, and diminished global standing. To commemorate it on currency would be to enshrine division and decline. To stamp “Global Britain” onto banknotes would be to enshrine a failed slogan — a post‑Brexit fantasy that collapsed under the weight of reality.

The hedgehog, by contrast, offers a soft distraction — a way of saying “look at our countryside” instead of “look at our politics.” 

The Royal Family’s Waning Aura
Traditionally, monarchs have anchored Britain’s banknotes. But Charles III inherits a monarchy stripped of mystique. Scandals, accusations of privilege, and the Harry‑Meghan rupture have exposed the institution as brittle. Younger generations increasingly question why unelected royals should symbolize the nation at all. To plaster Charles or his heirs across new notes would only remind the public of the monarchy’s contested legitimacy.  

Wildlife as Consensus
So the Bank of England turns to animals. Hedgehogs, owls, salmon — creatures that cannot divide opinion. They are symbols of conservation, not controversy. But this retreat into apolitical imagery is itself political. It reveals a state unable to celebrate its leaders, unwilling to confront its divisions, and embarrassed by its institutions.  

What the Hedgehog Really Says
The hedgehog on Britain’s money is not a celebration of nature. It is a confession: that the country’s politics are too toxic, its monarchy too fragile, and its national identity too contested to risk putting a human face on its currency. Britain has chosen the hedgehog because it has run out of people it can trust to symbolize itself.

text:
The Indian Army was facing severe interference from Chinese jammers along the border, and top engineers had failed to solve it.

That is when Sarvesh Sharma, the son of a daily-wage labourer built a drone in his home, prompting the Ministry of Defence to offer him a grant of ₹3.5 crore under the iDEX (Innovations for Defence Excellence) and DIO (Defence Innovation Organisation) programmes.

Keeping watch over enemies across snow-covered mountains like Siachen and Galwan is extremely difficult because China hacks our drones' GPS systems there.

Sarvesh, a computer engineering student at Government Polytechnic College, Hamirpur, Himachal Pradesh, spent ₹87,000 of his own money to build a drone named Rudra Edge T-1, capable of flying even in sub-zero temperatures.

Its greatest strength is its ability to bypass enemy radars and defeat any jamming system. Hacking it is virtually impossible.

When senior army officials witnessed this labourer's son’s talent, they were astonished. The government immediately granted him ₹3.5 crore so he could produce it on a large scale for the armed forces.

We salute this young man who overcame poverty to strengthen the nation's security.

text:
On December 15, 1979, twenty-one-year-old Alan Jackson stood at the altar of First Baptist Church in Newnan, Georgia, waiting to marry his high school sweetheart.

Denise was nineteen, wearing a modest white veil and looking toward a future with few guarantees. Alan had no record deal, no money, and no certainty that music would ever pay the rent. 

He was working as a forklift driver and mechanic around town, driving a worn-out car and playing local clubs on weekend nights whenever someone offered him a microphone.

When the moment arrived for the ceremony to follow traditional vows, Alan did something unexpected. Instead of a formal hymn or reading, he stepped toward the pulpit, took the church microphone into his hands, and sang "That's the Way" directly to Denise.

His fingers trembled around the stand as he started, his voice wavering before settling into the melody. Denise cried quietly beneath her veil, while parents and neighbors filled the wooden pews in silence, listening to an unpolished young singer who had never recorded a note in a Nashville studio.

That church performance predated the arena tours, the country music awards, and the sold-out stadium shows by more than a decade. 

Long before Denise handed a business card to Glen Campbell in an Atlanta airport terminal, she had already heard the voice that would fill arenas, singing to her first in a quiet hometown sanctuary 💕🎶

text:
Grok Bot's Multi-Model Routing: Agent Competition Is Shifting from Model Capability to Entrance Control

On October 7, 2026, Elon Musk announced on X that Grok Bot will no longer run only on SpaceXAI's own Grok models. It will use the best back-end model for any given task, including Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5, Midjourney, and Suno. "Whatever is most likely to give you the best outcome," Musk wrote. The announcement came one day after Grok users reported access problems on mobile and web services.

The routing layer is not the most profitable segment

OpenRouter routes AI applications to over 180 large language models from providers including Anthropic and OpenAI. It charges a 5.5% fee when users top up credits. Annualized revenue reached approximately $140 million by late July 2026, with gross margins around 71.5%. Stripe acquired OpenRouter for $7 billion in August 2026, a 50x multiple on $140 million of revenue.

The 71.5% gross margin looks high. But OpenRouter's $140 million annualized revenue is approximately 0.2% of Anthropic's $65 billion annualized revenue. The routing layer captures a small fraction of the traffic; the model layer owns the pricing power. Routing profit = transaction volume × take rate. The take rate faces compression: AWS Bedrock, Azure AI Foundry, and Google Vertex AI all offer multi-model access without a separate routing fee.

Grok Bot is not OpenRouter. Its revenue model is subscription — SuperGrok at $30 per month, SuperGrok Heavy at $300 per month. Users pay for "an AI colleague that completes tasks," not "an intelligent routing API." Routing is the implementation method, not the priced product.

The circular financing structure

Anthropic agreed in May 2026 to pay SpaceX nearly $45 billion over three years for computing resources — $1.25 billion per month through May 2029, with 90 days' notice for either party to end the agreement. The capacity comes from SpaceX's Colossus 1 and Colossus II data centers in Memphis, exceeding 300 megawatts.

This creates a circular path. SpaceX provides compute to Anthropic. Anthropic pays SpaceX compute fees. Grok Bot calls Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 API. SpaceX pays Anthropic API fees. SpaceX is simultaneously Anthropic's landlord and tenant. From a cash flow perspective, every dollar circulating through Grok Bot → Anthropic → SpaceX leaves a portion in the intermediate stage (Anthropic's model profit). But Grok Bot gains Claude Opus 5.5's reasoning capability, which its own models cannot provide in the near term.

The economic return of this routing strategy is not a routing take rate. It is distribution margin — controlling the user entrance while having upstream pricing power. If SpaceX obtains Claude API access at a discount below market public prices and provides Grok Bot to users on a subscription basis, the spread is the direct economic return.

Routing as independent infrastructure

Grok Bot's decision is not isolated. The decision layer is unbinding from the inference layer.

TypeSafe AI's Jev returns typed decisions with calibrated probabilities in roughly 70 to 500 milliseconds, at $0.042 per million input tokens with free output. It never generates text or code. The entire API is three question types — Choice, Score, and Noul.

AgentRouter, presented at ICML 2026, formalizes step-level model routing as a sequential assignment problem. Enterprise agent systems that route every LLM call to a frontier model waste 60-80% of their inference budget on subtasks that smaller models handle equally well. AgentRouter achieves 72% cost reduction relative to frontier-only baselines with less than 3% degradation in end-to-end task completion.

Gartner predicts that by the end of 2026, 40% of enterprise applications will embed task-specific AI agents, up from less than 5% a year earlier. Routing capability is becoming a standard component of enterprise AI deployment, not an independent fee layer.

Three paths in agent competition

Meta's Muse launched on September 8, 2026. It surpassed 5 million downloads in 22 days, faster than ChatGPT's 56 days, Grok's 103, and Claude's 492. It passed 3 million weekly users, with more than 1 million prompting daily. Meta's house ads helped — Muse took up to half of Meta's daily house ad impressions between September 14 and 27. Muse uses user data to train AI models by default; users can opt out in settings. It asks for control of a user's Gmail, calendar, and, on a Mac, the whole computer.

OpenAI announced Dots at DevDay 2026 on September 29. Each dot runs on GPT-6 Astra and gets its own cloud computer and web browser. It can plug into more than 4,000 apps. The first dot is included with Pro and Business Premium plans.

Grok Bot launched in beta on August 11, 2026, for SuperGrok Heavy, Cursor Ultra, and Cursor Team subscribers. Access widened to base SuperGrok at $30 per month by August 26. It opened to enterprises on September 3. Since late September, teams can publish shared Bots for colleagues to use in the app or Slack.

Data and trust as a structural constraint

When Grok Bot routes user tasks to third-party models, the data flow is an unresolved question. Musk did not specify which tasks go to which outside model, nor any data isolation or privacy protection measures.

Some early users have deleted such agents over privacy worries. One user told Business Insider he still uses Grok Bot but has not connected it to his email. Meta's Muse uses user data to train AI models by default. Amazon has blocked Muse from shopping on its site.

Privacy and trust are structural constraints on agent adoption at scale. Switching costs form when users route email, calendar, and file systems through an agent — but only if users trust the agent. If data flows are opaque, trust cannot be established.

Three variables to verify

First, whether Grok Bot's "other model" quota mechanism becomes a productized, separately priced offering. If it does, Grok Bot gains a routing-like revenue stream beyond subscriptions. If it remains hidden, routing is a cost center, not a revenue center.

Second, whether Muse and Dots user growth will slow in 2027. Muse's 5 million downloads were achieved with Meta's internal ad push. Dots' user numbers have not been disclosed.

Third, the API discount terms between SpaceX and Anthropic. If SpaceX obtains Claude Opus 5.5 API access below market public prices, Grok Bot's distribution margin has support. If at public prices, Grok Bot's subscription revenue may not cover third-party API costs.

Grok Bot's multi-model routing strategy is a strategic escalation that moves the competition dimension from the model layer to the entrance layer. It acknowledges that model capability is commoditizing and attempts to build a new moat by controlling the user entrance and having upstream pricing power. But the strategy's success depends on a simple fact: users will not pay because the backend is Claude instead of Grok. They pay because the agent understood the task and completed it. Routing quality is the means, not the end.

text:
The Diplomat piece by Taiwanese academic Ying-Yu Lin on China’s facility in Laos is a textbook case of alarmist framing divorced from geographic reality. Any rational person would know that Laos is landlocked, and Ban Keun Airport sits less than 500 kilometers south of Yunnan’s existing PLA Air Force bases. From a military standpoint, stationing fighters or AWACS there adds no new reach. The idea that this transforms China’s airpower projection is simply not credible.

First, the infrastructure is modest. A 2,000-meter runway is fine for training and light transport, but it is not optimized for sustained combat operations. There are no hardened shelters, layered defenses, or deep logistics. To call this a “strategic base” is to deliberately inflate its significance. It is a joint training center, nothing more.

Second, the geography makes the claim of maritime leverage laughable. Laos has no coastline. Ban Keun cannot directly support operations in the South China Sea or the Strait of Malacca. PLA aircraft already cover Southeast Asia from Yunnan. Moving them a few hundred kilometers south into Laos does not change the operational map.

Third, the real story here is political, not military. The facility embeds PLA presence in Laos, a client state already economically dependent on China. It integrates with the China–Laos Railway, giving Beijing continental logistics depth. That is about normalizing PLA activity in mainland Southeast Asia, not about airpower escalation. The Taiwanese researcher’s framing deliberately conflates political symbolism with operational capability.

Fourth, this narrative fits a broader pattern of cognitive warfare. By exaggerating PLA basing moves, Taiwan-linked analysts aim to alarm ASEAN and Washington, painting China as aggressively encircling the region. In reality, Ban Keun is not Djibouti, not Ream Naval Base, and not a game-changer. It is a symbolic foothold, useful for training Lao pilots and demonstrating political alignment, but militarily redundant.

Finally, the credibility gap is obvious. If you strip away the rhetoric, Ban Keun offers no new operational advantage beyond Yunnan. Its value lies in signaling and logistics, not in extending combat reach. To present it otherwise is to mislead.

In short: the article is less analysis than narrative construction. Ban Keun is about embedding presence and tightening Laos’ dependence, not about transforming PLA airpower. The exaggeration serves political ends, not military truth.

One thing is certain, the editorial team on the Diplomat have very low bar when it comes to reviewing credibility or suitability of articles to be accepted and published.

Hoosier Champions To Get National Spotlight On Friday

ANDERSON, Ind.—Oct. 7, 2025— Indiana Sire Stakes champions will be crowned on Friday, Oct. 9 at Harrah's Hoosier Park, with Indiana's best doing so under the national spotlight with FOX Sports 2 coverage from 8-11pm.

With over $2.4 million on the line during the 15-race program, seven of the eight $250,000 Indiana Sire Stakes Super Finals for two- and three-year-olds in races 7-13 will be featured during the FOX Sports window from 8-11 p.m. Vice President and General Manager of Racing, Gabe Prewitt, will be joined by Dave Weaver on-site to offer commentary to the national audience on the championship events which will feature to horses such as North America Cup champion, Odds On Mr Mamba.

First post for the Hoosier Champions card is 5:30 p.m. and will also include $70,000 Aged Sire Stakes Championships on the evening which features horses such as On To Norway, Little Rocket Man, and Can'ttouchthese. 

Bettors will also have a buffet of wagering options throughout the evening with $65,000 worth of guaranteed pools to take aim at including:

Race 1 - $10,000 Pick 5
Race 2 - $10,000 Pick 4
Race 6 - $10,000 Pick 4
Race 8 - $10,000 Pick 5
Race 12 - $15,000 Pick 4
Race 15 - $10,000 Hoosier High 5

In addition to the Indiana Sire Stakes finals, $50,000 Indiana Sire Stakes consolations will make up the remainder of the Friday card. The remainder of the consolations will take place on Saturday, Oct. 10 in addition to the $70,000 Mare Trot Sire Stakes Final which will serve as a non-betting race prior to the Saturday program at 5:15 p.m.

Free online racing programs for the Hoosier Champions card are available on the Hoosier Park website in addition to complimentary access to race replays. Qualifier replays are made available on the Hoosier Park AV YouTube channel.

text:
⟦ አሰብ · FILE 22/26 ⟧
▸▸▸ WHAT IT MEANS

Step back and the arc is striking.

◆ 2015: Djibouti pushes the UAE away; Eritrea takes it in
◆ 2015–2019: Assab becomes a war hub, quietly paid for in cash and fuel
◆ 2018: Assab is pitched as Ethiopia's road back to the sea, under Emirati patronage
◆ 2019–2021: the war ends for the UAE, and the base is packed up
◆ 2023–2026: Sudan's war puts the UAE and Eritrea on opposite sides
◆ Sept 2026: Asmara calls Abu Dhabi imperialist; Washington lets Eritrea's sanctions lapse
◆ 1 Oct 2026: Addis and Asmara close their embassies
◆ 5 Oct 2026: Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia and Sudan declare for the Red Sea littoral states — with Ethiopia the one regional power that is not one

Three lessons:

1️⃣ Red Sea bases follow the war of the moment. Assab mattered to Abu Dhabi because of Yemen. When Yemen ended for the UAE, so did most of Assab's value.

2️⃣ Gulf partnerships in the Horn are transactional. The patron of 2018's peace is now accused of fueling the Sudan war that divides its former partners.

3️⃣ Assab is now more important politically than militarily. It's mostly quiet, but it's at the center of the question Ethiopians keep asking: how does a country of over 120 million get back to the sea?

▸ AND THE ANSWER THAT ARRIVED THIS WEEK

On 4 October, Somalia's president said publicly that Ethiopia can use a Somali port — but must negotiate for it.

An offer, from the country that signed a defence pact with Cairo, made two days before Abiy spoke about sea access again.

▸ THE PORT WAS ALWAYS AVAILABLE BY AGREEMENT

What was never available was taking one.

▸ SO HERE IS THE WHOLE FILE IN ONE LINE

Ethiopia needs the sea. Eleven years of other people's wars, bases and declarations have not brought it one metre closer.

The one offer on the table this week came from a neighbour, across a table, with conditions.

That was always the only door. It was open the entire time.

I spoke directly with Alberta Prosperity Project co-founder Dennis Modry about the Washington meetings at the centre of The Globe and Mail’s recent investigation.

His account challenges much of the article’s most consequential framing.

The meetings with U.S. State Department representatives were real. So were the discussions about a possible future relationship between an independent Alberta and the United States.

But Modry says they were exploratory “Day 2” conversations — not negotiations, not campaign coordination, and not an offer of Alberta’s resources in exchange for American support.

My new article lays out his account, the meeting chronology, the eight-page discussion paper, and where the public record differs from The Globe’s narrative.

What must happen in the offseason:

1) Fire Tim Hyers - no doubter
2) STRONGLY consider moving on from Acuña. We could get a haul for him and at this point, both sides need to part ways
3) Trade for Elly De La Cruz. After trading Acuña, we could send a package that Cinninati would have to listen to.
4) Bring back Albies as a DH

6) Shop Riley (eat half of his contact if you have to)

9) Revisit a DeGrom trade. Maybe he’ll have changed his mind.
10) Usher in a youth movement to reinvigorate the older guys. If not traded, Southisene, Lodise, Hartman, and Caminiti are too good to be sitting in the minors waiting for an opportunity. They should be given every opportunity to make the team coming out of spring training.
11) Bring back Ron Washington at all costs. We desperately need him back to work with what should be a young middle infield and to coach third base. 

All in all, this was a predictable outcome. We didn’t have a third starter that EVERYBODY BUT AA knew we needed and it finally caught up to us. Offense disappeared when it mattered most. Harris and Albies were the only ones who showed up. Every other offensive player should be ashamed of themselves. AA should be fired, but if he’s not, he’s got A LOT to do to fix this shitty lineup. Star names all over the place with zero idea how to hit given certain situations. 

I doubt there is baseball next year. But if there is, we better see a VERY different team.

Asmara treats its own sovereignty as untouchable, yet for three decades it has hosted or backed Ethiopian armed movements, from the OLF and Ginbot 7 to TPDM, ONLF and ARDUF, as UN reports cited by Horn Review document. Now Ethiopia's Government Communication minister has told Bloomberg that Eritrean forces in Tigray must leave Ethiopian territory without delay.

Sovereignty is not a shield for one man to export war while denying his own citizens a vote. Real sovereignty includes reciprocity: respecting our neighbours' borders as firmly as we demand respect for our own. The PFDJ cannot offer that, because it answers to no parliament, no election and no implemented constitution.

EBRF is building the alternative: elected chapter structures, organizing in Ethiopia, diplomacy in Washington, and a peaceful, time limited transition to a constitutional government that defends Eritrea's borders and deals with its neighbours through diplomacy instead of proxies.

text:
Mike Malone on the #UNC #Tarheels coaching job: It's more than just basketball! - 10.7.26

📷 Michael Malone Discusses UNC Basketball, Recruiting, Team Development and Coaching Philosophy
📷 International recruiting whirlwind: UNC head coach Michael Malone described extensive international travel during his first three months, including trips to France, Spain, Portugal, Turkey and Mexico. An impromptu trip to Spain helped UNC recruit Sion Kéïta, illustrating the differences between college and NBA coaching.
📷 Adjusting to college basketball: Malone called his first two months a whirlwind of recruiting, hiring assistants, assembling a roster and adjusting to Chapel Hill. He said coaching on the practice court remains the most enjoyable and rewarding part of his job.
📷 Cameron Boozer's eligibility situation: The transcript identifies the player as Cameron F., whose eligibility remains unresolved. Malone confirmed the player would miss Friday's exhibition despite practicing daily and expressed hope for a prompt resolution. The player's full name and status should be verified before publication.
📷 Managing young players' workloads: Malone emphasized that coaching 17- and 18-year-olds requires greater attention to academic schedules, recovery, physical demands and personal well-being than coaching NBA professionals.
📷 Patience with player development: Malone acknowledged having to adjust his expectations after 25 years in the NBA. College players require more individual instruction, repetition and encouragement, but he finds their improvement particularly rewarding.
📷 Positionless basketball philosophy: UNC will use multiple players to initiate offense rather than relying on a traditional point guard. Terrence Brown, Henri Veesaar and several other guards and wings are expected to share ball-handling responsibilities.
📷 Defense and rebounding come first: Malone said his primary concerns are defensive stops, rebounding, limiting turnovers, sharing the basketball and improving teammates rather than determining who plays specific positions.
📷 Three exhibition games provide valuable tests: UNC's exhibitions against USC, Indiana and Charlotte will allow Malone to evaluate combinations, experiment with strategies and establish the team's identity before the regular season.
📷 Reconnecting with Carolina basketball tradition: Malone wants to honor UNC's history by welcoming former Tar Heels back to Chapel Hill, including coaches Wes Miller and King Rice, while maintaining relationships with former players.
📷 Former players reunite: More than 150 former Carolina basketball players attended a reunion organized to strengthen connections across generations. Malone particularly enjoyed meeting Charlie Scott, Jimmy Black and Bobby Jones.
📷 Former Tar Heels remain involved: Malone praised the willingness of former players, including Tyler Hansbrough, to attend practices and support the program. He believes their involvement helps current players and recruits understand Carolina's basketball tradition.
📷 Recruiting 'connectors': Malone wants selfless players who make teammates better. He cited LeBron James and Nikola Jokić as examples of elite players who elevate everyone around them.
📷 Leadership remains a work in progress: With 11 newcomers and five returning players, UNC is still developing its leadership structure. Malone wants players to hold one another accountable rather than depending entirely on the coaching staff.
📷 Different leadership styles are valuable: Malone said effective leaders do not necessarily need to be vocal. Some lead through their actions, while others motivate teammates through communication and accountability.
📷 High expectations for Neoklis Avdalas: Malone praised the Greek transfer's size, court vision, passing ability and unselfishness. He believes Avdalas can become an important contributor after improving his strength and conditioning.
📷 Sion Kéïta's impressive adjustment: Malone described the young international recruit's transition from Mali and Barcelona to Chapel Hill as remarkable. He praised his maturity, adaptability, length, athletic ability and potential.
📷 Jarin Stevenson's offensive development: Malone wants Stevenson to become more aggressive offensively through transition opportunities, post mismatches, offensive rebounds and attacks toward the basket.
📷 Respecting individual personalities: Malone emphasized that Stevenson should not be forced into becoming an outspoken or emotional leader. Instead, the coaching staff wants him to demonstrate confidence and aggression through his performance.
📷 Practice statistics guide coaching: UNC charts practice performances, including shot attempts and turnovers, to identify improvement opportunities and hold players accountable.
📷 Playing fast without playing carelessly: Malone wants an up-tempo offense built around disciplined decisions. He emphasized that speed cannot come at the expense of ball security or shot selection.
📷 Turnovers are a major concern: Malone stressed that successful teams cannot afford self-inflicted mistakes, declaring, "Good teams don't beat themselves."
📷 Daily improvement over championship talk: Malone said UNC's primary objective is building winning habits through productive practices rather than repeatedly discussing championship aspirations.
📷 Preparing for postseason success: Malone believes consistent daily improvement will put the Tar Heels in a stronger position when conference tournament and postseason competition arrive.
📷 Official recruiting visits offer personal connections: Malone joked about recruits' appetites and the number of Chapel Hill restaurants he has visited. More importantly, he sees campus visits as opportunities for recruits and families to experience the program firsthand.
📷 Authenticity drives recruiting: Malone refuses to change his personality when recruits attend practice. He believes honesty, approachability and genuine relationships help prospective players determine whether UNC is the right fit.
📷 Lessons from an NBA championship: Drawing on his championship experience in Denver, Malone wants to establish a culture where players work extremely hard while enjoying basketball and their relationships with teammates.
📷 Influential coaching mentors: Malone credited his father, Jeff Van Gundy, Mike Brown, Monty Williams and Gregg Popovich with shaping his coaching philosophy.
📷 Defense and attention to detail: Malone identified Van Gundy's defensive principles and meticulous preparation as particularly influential in developing his own coaching approach.
📷 Empowering assistant coaches: Lessons from Mike Brown helped Malone understand the importance of trusting assistants, giving them meaningful responsibilities and allowing them to contribute to decisions.
📷 Gregg Popovich's lasting advice: Malone recalled Popovich encouraging him to remain authentic while ensuring players understand that demanding coaching comes from genuine care and respect.
📷 Overall takeaway: Malone's first UNC team will emphasize defensive accountability, rebounding, disciplined up-tempo basketball, unselfish play and daily improvement. Although eligibility questions, roster chemistry and leadership remain unresolved, Malone believes the program is making progress toward establishing a sustainable winning culture.

Global News Brief  
1. Just The News: American-Israeli student Sophie Shabot has filed a federal lawsuit accusing New York City’s New School of failing to protect her from antisemitic harassment, intimidation and physical assaults. She alleges protesters shoved and spat on her, blocked her access to campus facilities and disrupted a Jewish student event, while administrators ignored complaints supported by photographs and videos. The lawsuit also alleges then-President Donna Shalala praised and financially supported encampment participants. Represented by the Lawfare Project, Shabot seeks damages for alleged discrimination and other violations; the claims have not been established in court.

2. News 13 Florida: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency in 25 counties ahead of Tropical Storm Isaias, which could strengthen into a hurricane. Forecasters projected landfall between Mississippi and the Florida Panhandle late Friday or early Saturday, prompting preparations across the Panhandle and Big Bend regions.

3. AP: Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella offered legal assistance Tuesday to Colombian military veterans accused in the 2021 assassination of Haitian President Jovenel Moïse. The veterans were recently extradited from Haiti to Florida after their case stalled for years.

4. Fortune Magazine: The U.S. spent $30 billion to ditch textbooks for laptops and tablets: The result is that Gen Z is the first generation since the late 1800’s to be less cognitively capable than their parents.

5. BBC: Malaysia has deported about 1,500 Myanmar nationals, including children, as the first phase of a plan to return 5,000 people, citing financial and security pressures. Authorities say the returns are voluntary, but the UN and human rights groups question whether people taken from immigration detention could freely consent and warn they could face persecution, forced conscription and violence in Myanmar. Amnesty International also raised concerns that the arrangement could help Myanmar’s military-backed government regain international legitimacy.

6. Al Jazeera: An explosion and fire forced Venezuela’s second-largest oil refinery, Cardon, to suspend operations. Reuters reported that the blaze began in a gas line at the facility in Punto Fijo, Falcón state, which can process 300,000 barrels of oil per day.

7. People: A man arriving from Cuba was arrested at Miami International Airport after customs officers noticed an unusual bulge and allegedly discovered 10 live birds in plastic tubes concealed in his underwear. According to a criminal complaint, Alberto Hernandez Castillo had declared no wildlife and lacked the required import documents. He was charged with smuggling goods, released on a $25,000 bond and is scheduled for arraignment on October 26.

8. Al Jazeera: More than one million people in South Sudan could lose vital food and nutrition assistance in October unless new funding is secured, the World Food Programme warns. Food stocks at its Malakal logistics hub have plunged from 10,000 tonnes a year ago to under 300 tonnes, while about 3,000 refugees and returnees arrive from Sudan each week. Rising prices, conflict, drought and flooding are worsening hunger, while illegal checkpoints obstruct aid deliveries.

9. People: Drake’s representative has denied rumors that the rapper is expecting a child with his former girlfriend, Canadian singer Keshia Chanté. Chanté announced she is seven months pregnant with a boy but has not publicly identified the father, prompting speculation online. Drake already shares a son, Adonis, with artist Sophie Brussaux.

10. ESPN: In the MLB playoffs, the White Sox swept the Astros and lead the Guardians 2–0, while the Yankees swept the Red Sox but trail the Rays 2–0. In the National League, the Braves eliminated the Phillies before falling behind the Dodgers 2–1, and the Padres swept the Cubs but trail the Brewers 2–1. The World Series begins October 23.

11. ESPN: The WNBA playoffs have reached the semifinals, with the New York Liberty facing the Atlanta Dream and the Las Vegas Aces taking on the Golden State Valkyries. Both series continue with Game 2 on October 7, as the four teams compete for a place in the championship round. The best-of-seven Finals begin October 17.

12. BBC: Amazon has secured worldwide streaming rights to the Emmy Awards under a six-year agreement, according to the BBC, moving the ceremony from traditional US broadcast networks to live global streaming.

13. Japan Today: U.S. Military Restrictions in Okinawa: U.S. forces in Okinawa imposed a night curfew and alcohol ban for troops following the arrest of a U.S. Marine on suspicion of a robbery-murder involving a local woman.

14. The Telegraph: British MI6 fears August Hanning, the former head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service, may have disclosed British secrets. Classified documents were reportedly found at his home following his arrest on suspicion of espionage and treason.

15. Washington Post: A California couple with at least 21 children, many born through surrogacy, has been charged with abusing at least 14 of them at their Arcadia mansion. Prosecutors allege Guojun Xuan and Silvia Zhang recruited surrogates under false pretenses and encouraged or participated in beatings by nannies, with abuse captured on surveillance cameras. The investigation began after a two-month-old baby suffered a head injury in 2025; the couple has pleaded not guilty.

16. The Guardian: Finnish authorities have ordered Google to halt preparatory work at two planned data centres in Muhos and Kajaani until environmental assessments are completed. The order follows extensive forest clearance, including 330 hectares in Muhos, before the required reviews were finished. The sites form part of Google’s €13 billion investment in Finland. Google acknowledged falling short of its standards and said it would follow regulators’ guidance.

17.  Wall Street Journal: A small group of young American Jews has moved to Israel since October 7, enlisting in the military, marrying and building lives despite the war. Their arrivals contrast with record emigration: nearly 270,000 Israeli citizens left between 2023 and 2025, about 50% more than during the comparable period a decade earlier, including doctors, engineers and other highly educated professionals.

18. NY Times: Henri Kagan of France and Kenso Soai of Japan have been awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for discovering nonlinear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis, advancing understanding of how reactions produce molecules with a particular “handedness.”

19.  L.A. Times: Californians face some of the nation’s highest water bills, with rates in some areas exceeding 2.5 times the national average, according to a new report. Nationwide, average water bills rose 62% between 2015 and 2025—1.6 times faster than overall inflation and twice as fast as grocery prices.

20. Epoch News: Russia faces growing international scrutiny after Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old technician at Siberia’s Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute, died on October 2 from severe pneumonia. Reports linking her death to pneumonic plague or a laboratory accident remain unconfirmed. The WHO is seeking urgent clarification about a second employee reportedly hospitalized with pneumonia of unknown origin; a second death has not been confirmed.

21. NY Post: Starbucks is reportedly closing 250 stores this week, including 17 in New York, according to the New York Post.

text:
$QCOM v $ARM 

Lets start today's tweets with the bench trial over the last 3 days becuase it got spicy at the end of today (day 3).

To set the stage (You can read some of my previous tweets explaining why some things are being tried to the judge) the jury goes home around 4:30 p.m. each afternoon, the trial continues and shifts right into the bench trial to handle Qualcomm's equitable claims and California Unfair Competition Law claims. Day 1 of the bench trial kicked off with brief opening statements from both sides on the California UCL standards under Epic v. Apple and Cel Tech, arguing over whether Qualcomm has to define a rigid antitrust market or whether the broader unfair competition and competitor tests apply.

Day 1 of the bench trial kicked off with brief opening statements from both sides on the California UCL standards under Epic v. Apple and Cel Tech, arguing over whether Qualcomm has to define a rigid antitrust market or whether the broader unfair competition and competitor tests apply. 

From there Isaacson put Cristiano back on the stand. Amon walked through the history of the 2013 ALA, explaining how Qualcomm has always operated under a flat $1.88 cap per chip for v8 and v9. He contrasted that with Arm's new v10 proposal, which abandons the per chip cap and demands either a percentage of the entire chip selling price or a per core fee multiplied across every core. Amon pointed out that Qualcomm's datacenter chip built for Meta has 288 cores. The second Isaacson asked for the specific proposed core dollar rate, Arm objected, and Judge Noreika opted not to clear the gallery. (At this time there was a sidebar where I assume the numbers were discussed privately at the bench).

Once they stepped back from the bench, Amon explained how Arm's proposed terms put Qualcomm at a massive competitive disadvantage against Nvidia's Grace and Vera datacenter CPUs and against Arm's own in house silicon initiatives. On cross, LoCascio grilled Amon on whether Qualcomm really expected to pay the same $1.88 whether a chip had five cores or 288 cores, and pushed him on whether other licensees accept segmented pricing by market tier before the court adjourned for the night.

Day 2 of the bench trial saw Amon wrap up his testimony, and then things got spicy when the General called Lynn Couillard, Arm's Senior Director who manages Qualcomm's sales account. Couillard needed to catch a flight so they took her direct examination right away. 

Dunn's goal was transparent from the jump, she was building a California extrinsic evidence record to prove that Qualcomm validly elected to extend its 2013 ALA to cover future architectures like v10 back in May 2020 under Section 14.1.B, and that Arm internally knew it was valid. Dunn pulled up internal emails from 2020 where Qualcomm gave written notice to extend to v9 next, and Couillard forwarded it to Arm leadership calling the move clever and admitting she saw no reason why the election could not hold. 

Couillard tried to hide behind deposition amnesia, claiming over and over that she did not recall her thought process or what she meant. Judge Noreika got visibly fed up with the pacing, complaining that Dunn was reading deposition snippets to a witness who claimed she remembered nothing, and bluntly warned Dunn that it was boring, not effective, and that her time was ticking. But Dunn stuck to her guns and ground out the admissions she neede  Couillard to conceded that v9 next meant the generation following v9 which is v10, and admitted she told Arm colleagues she saw no reason the election would not hold.

Dunn then called Renee Haas back to the stand and immediately confronted him with PTX 236, an internal 2018 record where Arm licensing executives David Bettesworth and Chris Hodgson explicitly concluded that Qualcomm had the contractual right to extend to v10 and v11 within seven years of the 2013 ALA. Haas was forced to admit that when Qualcomm exercised that exact right in 2020, he wrote an email five minutes later claiming it could not hold.

Dunn then went for the kill by asking Haas to name the five companies that currently hold active architecture licenses covering v10 or future architectures. Haas balked in open court, stating that identifying those licensees was far too sensitive for a public forum. LoCascio immediately moved to seal the courtroom under the Third Circuit standard, arguing that public disclosure would compromise customer relationships and confidential competitive terms. (At this point they cleared the courtroom and sealed the proceedings for the rest of the day to take the testimony). 

Now on day 3 (today) court ran late into the evening, wrapping up just after 6:00 p.m. with an absolute spectacle between Judge Noreika and Arm CEO Rene Haas.

Before calling Haas back, Isaacson squeezed in two minutes with Jonathan Weiser to enter PTX 86. That email was pure gold for Qualcomm. It showed Arm EVP of worldwide sales Antonio Viana explicitly telling Qualcomm in 2012 that both sides expected to negotiate an extension at the 7.5 year mark including v10. LoCascio tried to cross Weiser on Qualcomm requesting an urgent amendment in May 2020 right before the deadline, but the contemporaneous record is now locked in Arm knew from day one that v10 was meant to be included.

Then the General called Rene Haas back to the stand, and Apple counsel Hannah Cannon spent the next fifteen minutes popping up like a jack in the box. Dunn pulled up PTX 1004, confronting Haas with public reporting that Apple pays a flat fee of less than 30 cents per chip regardless of core count, and extends beyond 2040. Apple counsel and LoCascio instantly objected, demanding to seal the courtroom again. Judge Noreika noted that Apple counsel was popping up way more than she cared to and offered to clear the room, but the General agreed to move along to keep the clock moving without another sealed session.

Dunn then pulled up PTX 642, an October 2022 executive deck that Haas and Masayoshi Son presented to Samsung. The presentation pitched building a joint super chip and vertically integrating Arm with Samsung, right around the exact same time Masa was privately telling Samsung executives that Qualcomm's ALA was expiring in 2025. Dunn then used Arm opening slides to pin Haas down. In order to actually know whether Qualcomm was demanding the lowest rate in each market tier, one would have to see the actual confidential agreements.

LoCascio did a direct of Haas to push Arm defense. Haas claimed Arm never negotiates off a menu card, argued Apple is a unique OEM with its own captive software stack, and explained that Nvidia 20 year extension was part of the two billion dollar merger breakup fee. Haas argued that 2013 rates were designed for twenty dollar phone chips with four cores, whereas modern server chips sell for thousands of dollars and have hundreds of cores.

Then came the main event. Judge Noreika took over questioning, and things went completely off the rails for Arm.

Judge Noreika pressed Haas on why he and Cristiano Amon had a 45 minute meeting in July talking about hypotheticals, bluntly telling Haas that two powerful CEOs sitting around talking about hypotheticals sounded like a complete waste of time. Haas admitted under oath that it was indeed a waste of time.

Then Judge Noreika pointed out that Haas testified to the jury that Arm wants Qualcomm to succeed, but confronted him with internal emails and messages where Arm called Qualcomm the enemy and plotted to terminate the contract. Judge Noreika looked Haas in the eye and asked why she should believe him when she has seen rough documents behind the scenes showing the exact opposite, warning him point blank that the jury is looking at those documents and it does not look good for Arm.

LoCascio scrambled to rehabilitate his witness, prompting Haas to blame the hostility on lingering anger over the Nuvia deal. Haas admitted he felt angry and betrayed by Qualcomm. When Judge Noreika asked whether that anger is still poisoning the relationship, Haas conceded that there is certainly residue of it.

Dunn stepped up and confronted Haas with Arm internal projections showing that by 2030, two thirds of Arm revenue, roughly fifteen billion dollars, is projected to come from selling its own chips. Haas got visibly defensive, claiming Jensen Huang at Nvidia and cloud CEOs congratulated him on the launch, and argued that the court does not decide who his competitors are.

Dunn fired back that the court decides whether Arm is doing a bad thing under unfair competition laws, and asked the ultimate question given that Arm will be competing directly against chipmakers while serving as their licensor, does Haas believe Arm alone should decide what royalty rates its competitors pay.

Haas walked straight into the trap, arrogantly declaring It is our product, of course we should decide, who else, if we do not decide, who should decide.

With that jaw dropping admission of monopoly power on the record, Dunn passed the witness, and Judge Noreika abruptly adjourned. Popcorn all around.
